INTRODUCTION Groin injuries are a common issue and concern among athletes, particularly those participating in sports that require sudden changes in direction, kicking, or high accelerating intensity movements. These injuries can be difficult to diagnose and treat as well as rehabilitate. Large muscle groups play a part in a joint ’ s stability. 1,2 Today’ s collegiate athletes may be predisposed to inju- ries related to increased size, mass, acceleration, and torque thereby leading to forces five times greater than their body weight. 3–7 The groin or medial thigh musculature components are both directly and indirectly an essential component to hip stability. 2 Commonly reported injury mechanisms include forced adduction, twisting, adductor extension, and/or eccentric adductor failure from reactive ground forces.8–11 The earliest reported groin adductor strain was described in Irish bowling. 12 Other adductor strains/groin injuries have a reported incidence of 5% to 23% observed mainly in soccer, ice hockey, and a few other sports. 13 In American football, this prevalence of groin strain/injuries has ranged from 0.4% to 12%; however, there are distinct differences in the injury tracking and reporting techniques used, potentially due to the limited available data specifically reporting adductor injuries coming from investigations before 1992 or after 2018. 7,14–19 These differences may partly explain the large variability in reported injury preva- lence and this investigation aims to improve our under- standing of adductor trauma at the collegiate level of play by providing an observation period longer than previous investigations. 18,19 Prior literature indicates a greater reinjury risk with increasing competitive levels. 8,11,20,21 More severe inju- ries such as adductor-related avulsion fractures 22 can cause significant time loss with an average return to play of 4.8 months, even up to 8 months in various sports.23 There are public health concerns from groin related injuries as well. Over one third of National Bas- ketball Association players report groin pain following retirement, and 47% have related anxiety, depression, lower physical activity levels, and decreased quality of life. 24 Across a variety of sports, males in higher level collision activities may be predisposed to higher levels of hip osteoarthritis, which in turn may lead to increased rates of surgical treatment procedures. 25–27 The most current classification for groin-related inju- ries was provided by the Doha consensus agree- ment.28 The classification system defined four main entities for groin pain: (1) adductor-related — the most common, (2) iliopsoas related, (3) inguinal related groin— no inguinal hernia present, and (4) pubic related— pubic symphysis bone and surrounding tissue tenderness. Based on these criteria, this prospective data analysis and subsequent discussion concentrates more specifically on the adductor-related groin injuries. PURPOSE With the potential impact of groin trauma on an athlete ’ s physical and mental health, further research is war- ranted. Therefore, based on (1) the excessive physical demands placed on the body by American football, (2) the multiple array of movements performed by the groin, and (3) the potential long-term reduction in qual- ity of life, the purpose of this study will be to quantify the long-term prevalence and etiology of groin injuries during game-related National Collegiate Athletic Asso- ciation (NCAA) football competition across artificial and natural grass surfaces. It was hypothesized that college football athletes would not experience any difference in surface-related groin trauma while competing on either artificial or natural grass surfaces. METHODS Population A total of 41 universities competing in the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) were evaluated for game-related groin injuries sustained on either an artificial turf infill system or natural grass surface over the course of 16 competitive se

Following an open invitation to all FBS universities that met the criteria for inclusion, interested head ATCs for each university were approached because of their daily interaction with the athletes and coaches during and after sport trauma and their expertise in injury rec- ognition. 29,30 Prior to the football season, the respective ATCs were provided with an overview of the purpose and procedures of the study, copies of the injury sur- veillance form, and detailed instructions for comple- tion to avoid the potential for performance and detection biases. 31,35 Communication was main- tained to discuss potential concerns and ensure accuracy of collection, comprehensiveness of infor- mation, and ease of application. 36 The protocol was approved by the institutional review board at the uni- versity in which the study was based, and the study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines for the use of human subjects as stipulated by the Ameri- can College of Sports Medicine. 37 All regular-season, postseason playoff champion- ships, and bowl games were included. Injury data was recorded following game completion and submitted in a timely manner (the vast majority of forms were com- pleted within 1 week), with additional support from ATC notes to avoid lapse of memory leading to inac- curacy or response distortion. 29,35 All game-related injuries were evaluated by the attending head ATC and team physicians on site and subsequently in the physician’ s office when further follow-up and treatment were deemed necessary. Any sport trauma that occurred toward the end of the competition schedule was monitored beyond the player ’ s specific season to determine the date of recovery and functional return to play. 29,38 Completed injury surveillance forms containing minor trauma were emailed to the author within 7 working days after a game and were processed before the next game. More serious injuries with extended time loss were submitted upon diagnostic completion. A follow-up telephone visit was used to obtain any additional information pertaining to any changes or additions in diagnosis, treatment, or time to return to play. To avoid the potential for on- the-field detection bias, 31 a single-blind outcome approach was maintained throughout the study period, with total data collected restricted to the ATCs and data compilation and analysis limited to the pri- mary investigators. Definitions The definition of injury was based on a combination of functional outcome, observation, and treat- ment. 29,30,34 A reportable injury was defined as any game-related football trauma reported or treated by the ATC or physician that resulted in an athlete miss- ing all or part of a game. 16,32 Injury severity was based on the number of days absent from practice or game competition (time loss). As previously described, any trauma that required 0 to 6 days of time loss was considered a minor injury . An injury that required 7 to 21 days of time loss resulting in the athlete being unable to return to play at the same competitive level was considered a substantial injury . Any trauma that required 22 or more days of time loss was considered a severe injury . 29 Regarding stage of injury , ac

touchdown, field goal, kickoff, punting, punt return, or fumble recovery. 16,29 To optimize cell size and enhance interpretation, the 23 player positions were condensed and analyzed by offense, defense, and special teams and by specific player skill position (quarterback, backfield, offensive line, tight end, receiver, defensive line, linebacker, sec- ondary).29,39 Each team ’ s ATC documented the type of cleat design (7-studded and 12-studded cleats, molded or hybrid cleats, edge or blade-style cleats, turf or elas- tomeric short rubber cleats) and the age of the playing surface.40 Environmental factors such as field conditions (no precipitation/dry field, rain, snow, sleet, no precipi- tation/wet field, adverse conditions combined) and envi- ronmental temperature (cold days ≤59 /C14 F, moderate days 60 –79/C14 F, hot days ≥80/C14 F) were obtained before game time and whenever an injury occurred; these data were obtained by the ATCs and/or through the local air- port climatic data. 7,41,42 Additionally, in-season and postseason imaging and surgical procedures (com- puted tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and radiography) were documented. Age of playing surface was defined as new fields, 1- to 3-year-old fields, and 4- to 7-year-old fields. Fields 8 or more years of age were condensed due to the expiration of the manufac- turer warranty. Statistical analysis Data were grouped by playing surface (artificial turf, natural grass) and tabular frequency distributions were computed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 28.0; Armonk, NY) software, with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) determined as described else- where. 43 Because most universities play approxi- mately 10 to 12 games each season, exposure to injury was defined in terms of team games, as previ- ously recommended. Injury incidence rate was expressed as injuries per 10 team games and calcu- lated as [( number of injuries /C4 number of team games ) /C2 10] as previously reported. 7,41 Data were then subjected to multivariate analyses of variance (MANOVAs) and Wilks λ criteria using general linear model procedures. 44 Effect sizes were reported in the context of the multivariate model using partial eta squared ( η2 p) and classified as small (η2 p ≥ 0:01), medium ( η2 p ≥ 0:06), and large ( η2 p ≥ 0:14) according to criteria previously established. 45,46 When significant main effects were observed, univariate post hoc procedures were performed. An experiment-wise type I error rate of .05 was established a priori , and least squared means procedures were required because of the uneven number of observations on which to compare differences between variables. RESULTS In sum, following 16 seasons of play, 2243 total games were documented with 1061 games (47.3%) played on a three-layer heavyweight artificial turf infill system and 1182 games (52.7%) played on natural grass. Of the 9360 total injuries, 4714 lower extremity injuries occurred across both surfaces. Of these, 111 adductor- related groin injuries were documented with 48 (43.2%) occurring on artificial turf, and 63 (56.8%) on natural grass. These 111 injuries comprised 1.2% of all injuries and 2.4% of lower extremity trauma. Surface type had a very small to moderate effect on any outcome of inter- est ( η 2 p ¼ :002 – 0:119). All groin trauma was attributed to standard play, with no injuries as a result of foul play or illegal action. As shown in Table 1, MANOVA indicated no signifi- cant surface effect by injury severity ( F2,108 = 0.511; p = .602). The majority of groin trauma involved minor injuries on both surfaces. MANOVAs also indicated no significant surface effect by injury classification (F 2,108 = 0.377; p = .687), injury category ( F1,109 = 0.850; p = .430), primary type of injury ( F4,106 = 0.293; p = .830), or injury mechanism ( F11,99 = 0.641; p = .776) (Table 2). The majority of adductor-related groin cases were acute and primarily occurred during shoe-surface noncontact play. The primary type of

these findings. 55–59 The majority of groin injuries among athletes wearing molded/hybrid cleats is likely a function of this cleat style being the most popular, mak- ing up 62% of the distribution in this study and 49% in another investigation examining >4000 injuries to American football athletes. 7 The key point to this study remains that, regardless of statistical findings, when based on a typical 10 –12 game college football season, the incidence of groin trauma as well as the influence of playing surface are minimal. This is substantiated by a single groin injury occurring every 1.8 seasons on natu- ral grass and a single groin injury occurring every 2.4 seasons on artificial turf. Regarding the implications of this study for perspec- tives in public health, the minimal difference in trauma across outcomes of interest indicates the need to shift focus to early detection and understanding long-term health outcomes following groin trauma. 24,60 The detri- mental effects that high-impact collisions have to the adductor-related groin area, that is, hip arthritis, depres- sion in American sports, highlight the importance of early detection to minimize the severity of progressive debilita- tion. 24–26,61 Following groin trauma, as stressed in recent studies, an athlete who engages in general lower body resistance exercise in the days following an acute injury can progress to adductor-specific training as part of a regular strength and conditioning program and effec- tively return to preinjury levels of performance. 62,63 Limitations There were potential limitations to the study that may have influenced the incidence of adductor-related groin injuries. influence of precompetition workloads 65,66; previous injury history, prior exposure to surface type during dif- ferent games, and associated medical procedures 67,68; quality of field maintenance 64,65; differences in postural or joint integrity, musculoskeletal structure, and biome- chanics of player movement 64,69; actual versus average time to exposure to injury 70; sports skill level, intensity of play, and fatigue level at time of injury 71;a na t h l e t e’ s avoidance in seeking help following injury 35,72;u n r e - ported congenital or developmental factors predisposing an athlete to additional injury 38,64; unforeseen mis- hap32,38; simply for an acute injury to go unre- ported16,32,73; or a concomitant undiagnosed other type of groin injury. 28 Although prior injury may have had an effect on an acute injury, athletes were cleared for return to play based on criteria previously established. 74 Any variability in field quality could have been confounded by weather conditions as the season progressed. 75 Finally, opportunity to obtain data on long-term quality of life dif- ferences following trauma between the two surface groups was beyond the scope of this study. Key strengths of the study were the opportunity to follow a large number of FBS universities during the 16-year period, using prospective, validated methods that reduced fluctuations often observed in single- season injury patterns and individual team effect, 76,77 as well as minimized the over- and underestimation of sport trauma observed in publicly obtained data- bases. 71,73,78 In addition, the combined method of assessing functional outcome, direct observation, and treatment records as well as the daily interac- tions of ATCs in direct communication with athletes in this study minimized the potential for transfer bias and unreported injuries throughout the season. 29,70 In totality, these efforts enhanced the ability to iden- tify adductor-related groin injury incidence and possi- ble differences between artificial and natural grass fields. The influence of risk factors other than an artificial turf versus natural grass field cannot be overlooked. Because of inherent challenges of collecting data on multiple indices and on numerous teams and players over an extended period of time, the degree of influ- ence from these risk factors remains a limitation that can only be acknowledged at this time 16,70 However, the prospective cohort multivariate design enhanced sample size, controlled for seasonal and team varia- tion, and allowed for greater insight into the subtle dif- ferences in adductor-related groin injuries at the collegiate level of play. CONCLUSION In collegiate football, heavyweight artificial turf was found to be as safe as natural grass with respect to adductor-related groin injuries. The hypothesis that surface type would not affect groin injury rates was sup- ported, with no meaningful difference in injury incidence between artificial and natural grass surfaces. Further research is warranted to elucidate the link between groin trauma and long-term adverse health outcomes and to determine if these results are generalizable to other levels of football competition.
